clue.text: Dizzy glory of an April day

definitions.text: Dizzy glory of an April day

parts.words: Dizzy glory of an April day
parts.note: Dizzy was the nickname of Benjamin Disraeli, whose favourite flower is worn on 19 April, the day of his death, so the clue reads as the bloom that is that day's glory

explanation.surface: A spring day so lovely it makes the head spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dizzy' looks like giddiness, but it is Disraeli, the Victorian prime minister; 19 April was kept as a day in his memory, when his supporters wore his favourite yellow spring flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The pale yellow spring bloom was Disraeli's favourite flower and the emblem of his memorial day in April.

clue.text: Not much room for Jemima to swim

definitions.text: Not much room for Jemima to swim

parts.words: Not much room for Jemima to swim
parts.note: Jemima is Beatrix Potter's duck, whose surname is a small pool of rainwater, hardly room for a swim

explanation.surface: A girl called Jemima complaining that the pool is too small.
explanation.walkthrough: Jemima is Jemima Puddle-Duck from Beatrix Potter's children's books.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pool of rainwater on the ground is too shallow to swim in, and it is also Jemima the duck's surname.

clue.text: Fabricate an opening in the first place

indicators.note: in the first place says the little word in stands at the front

parts.note: taken as written
a vent is an opening for air or gas

explanation.surface: Advice to make up an excuse for a gap in the first instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the first place' looks like 'originally', but it is an order instruction: the word 'in' is set at the front of the opening.
explanation.definitionFit: To fabricate is to make up or devise something, especially something new or false.

clue.text: The river rose, of course, when this burst

definitions.text: The river rose, of course, when this burst

indicators.note: burst tells us the letters of river and rose break apart and re-form

explanation.surface: A flood explained: the river level climbed because a dam gave way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay: a burst water store makes the river rise.
explanation.definitionFit: A dam-held lake storing water would flood a river if its wall gave way.

clue.text: Bowdlerized version of Lady Macbeth's bloodstain? (Not Much Ado)

definitions.text: Bowdlerized version of Lady Macbeth's bloodstain? (Not Much Ado)

parts.words: Bowdlerized version of Lady Macbeth's bloodstain? (Not Much Ado)
parts.note: Lady Macbeth cries 'Out, damned spot!'; cleaned of the swear word, the damned mark becomes a mild phrase for a little trouble, not Much Ado About Nothing

explanation.surface: A censored edition of Shakespeare's Scottish play.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowdlerized means cleaned of rude words; 'damned spot' turns into the British understatement for a minor difficulty, while 'Not Much Ado' nods to another Shakespeare title.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom for a minor problem replaces 'damned' with something harmless, a small fuss rather than great trouble.

clue.text: A cure for hot-headedness ?

parts.note: hot-headedness reads as a temper, but taken literally a hot head is cooled by a frozen covering placed on top of it

explanation.surface: A remedy for someone with a quick temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for a calming influence on a quick temper; the literal reading wants something cold sitting on top of a head, the frozen covering at a pole or mountain summit.
explanation.definitionFit: A polar or mountain covering of permanent ice sits on the 'head' of the globe and keeps it frozen, a literal cure for heat up top.

clue.text: "Down the green hill athwart a cedarn ——" (Coleridge)

definitions.text: Down the green hill athwart a cedarn ——" (Coleridge)

parts.words: Down the green hill athwart a cedarn ——" (Coleridge)
parts.note: a line from Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan with its last word left blank for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A line of Romantic poetry describing a hillside of cedar trees.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a quotation with a blank: Kubla Khan's line runs 'Down the green hill athwart a cedarn' and ends with a word for a thicket.
explanation.definitionFit: In Coleridge's line the missing word means a thicket or woodland shelter, here one of cedar trees.

clue.text: Study sound impressions on parchments or hides

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart

indicators.note: sound tells us the word is given by how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: seals are wax impressions stamped on parchment documents

explanation.surface: A scholar examining wax marks on old documents or animal skins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective for good impressions; it says SEALS is heard, spelt CEALS.
explanation.definitionFit: To hide something is to keep it out of sight, to keep it secret.

clue.text: Request item by invitation

parts.note: formal invitations say that someone requests 'the ___ of your company', so the word is the thing requested in an invitation

explanation.surface: Asking for an object to be delivered by invitation only.
explanation.walkthrough: Formal invitations are worded 'requests the ___ of your company'; the missing word is the item requested.
explanation.definitionFit: The word that fills 'requests the ___ of your company' means delight or enjoyment.

clue.text: Arithmetic as a method of government ?

definitions.meaning: one of the four basic operations of sums, sharing a number into equal parts
the principle of 'divide and rule', and also the parliamentary vote in which members split into lobbies

explanation.surface: Treating sums as a way to run a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Splitting numbers is an arithmetic operation, and splitting opponents (or splitting members into voting lobbies) is a way of governing.

clue.text: A way of exploration

parts.note: a tree-lined road is a way, and a line of inquiry is called by the same word, as in exploring every possibility

explanation.surface: A route taken by an explorer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a broad street and a line of approach in an inquiry, as in 'explore every possible line'.

clue.text: A flag for Fort Knox ?

parts.note: a standard is a flag, and Fort Knox is the US bullion depository holding gold reserves

explanation.surface: Choosing a banner to fly over a US army base.
explanation.walkthrough: Fort Knox in Kentucky stores the US gold reserve; the answer is the monetary system tying currency to gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The monetary system backing currency with gold reserves suits Fort Knox, and a standard is also a flag.

clue.text: This landing was on the sea

definitions.text: This landing was on the sea

parts.words: This landing was on the sea
parts.note: the first crewed touchdown on the Moon in 1969 was in the Sea of Tranquility, a dark plain named as if it were water

explanation.surface: A seaplane or boat coming down on water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea' suggests water, but the Apollo 11 landing site was the Mare Tranquillitatis, the Sea of Tranquility, one of the Moon's dark plains.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apollo 11 Moon landing came down in the Sea of Tranquility, so it was a landing on a 'sea' of the Moon.

clue.text: Having lost the second half at table tennis? Rules do so change

definitions.text: Having lost the second half at table tennis?

indicators.note: the instruction that the rules do change tells us the letters of those three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint after losing the second half of a ping-pong match, with a grumble about altered rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Table tennis is also called ping-pong; lose the second half, 'pong' (a British word for a bad smell), and you are left without a smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ping-pong without its 'pong', British slang for a stink, leaves something with no smell at all.

clue.text: She turns the searchlight of her charms on Constable, it seems

definitions.text: She turns the searchlight of her charms on Constable, it seems

parts.words: She turns the searchlight of her charms on Constable, it seems
parts.note: a constable is a bobby, the British nickname for a policeman, and a woman whose charms shine on him like a searchlight blinds him with her glamour

explanation.surface: A glamorous woman aiming her charms at a painter named Constable.
explanation.walkthrough: Constable looks like the painter John Constable; read it as a police constable, a 'bobby', who is dazzled. The phrase is British slang for a stunning person or thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang term for a remarkable, eye-catching person literally describes someone who dazzles a policeman.

clue.text: His subject is a beastly one

definitions.text: His subject is a beastly one

parts.words: His subject is a beastly one
parts.note: beastly usually means nasty, but literally it means to do with beasts, the subject of animal science

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that his field of study is horrible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beastly' sounds like 'unpleasant', a schoolboy word; read literally, it means about animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientist who studies animals has beasts as the subject of his work.

clue.text: A star of note

parts.note: a famous star is a star of note, but in print a star-shaped mark points the reader to a footnote

explanation.surface: A celebrated performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A star of note' suggests a celebrity; it is a star-shaped printed mark that refers to a note.
explanation.definitionFit: The star-shaped typographical symbol is used to point to a footnote.

clue.text: A quiet little French girl to have for dinner ?

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
petite is the French word for little in its feminine form, as for a girl

explanation.surface: A shy, small French girl invited round for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at a dinner guest, or worse, a meal; what one actually has for dinner is a desire to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunger or relish for food is what a diner brings to the table, something one has at dinner.

clue.text: Pin-up for pickers, for one

parts.note: the rhyme 'see a pin and pick it up, all the day you'll have good luck' makes picking up a pin an example of a belief in luck

explanation.surface: A glamour photo admired by fruit pickers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pin-up' suggests a glamour picture; here it is a pin picked up off the floor for luck, as in the old British rhyme, an example of irrational belief.
explanation.definitionFit: Picking up a pin for good luck is one instance of an irrational belief in omens and charms.

clue.text: Smoothly getting a lion without a gun

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the lion's letters go round the gun

parts.note: Leo is the lion of the zodiac
gat is slang for a gun

explanation.surface: Bagging a lion with no rifle, quietly and with ease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but here has its old sense 'outside', so the lion goes around the gun. The answer is the musical term for smooth, connected playing.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical direction meaning played smoothly with notes joined together.

clue.text: Of which the herdsman is in control of course

definitions.text: Of which the herdsman is in control of course

parts.words: Of which the herdsman is in control of course
parts.note: a herdsman naturally controls young bullocks, and the same word means directs the course of a vehicle

explanation.surface: A cowman naturally in charge of his herd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but also says that someone directing a course controls it; the herdsman controls young castrated bulls.
explanation.definitionFit: Young castrated bulls are what a herdsman controls, and the same word means guides the direction of something.

clue.text: Non-stop "Go" musical

parts.note: non-stop means always, for ever
green is the traffic-light colour for go

explanation.surface: An advertisement for a lively show that never pauses.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a title: a 1930 London stage musical by Rodgers and Hart, filmed in 1934 with Jessie Matthews.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of a Rodgers and Hart stage show of 1930, later a film, so it is a musical.

clue.text: A part of every single benefice

definitions.text: A part of every single benefice

indicators.note: a part of says the answer is a run of letters within the words single benefice

explanation.surface: A remark that every church living includes a certain item.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines and hides the answer: each parish living traditionally came with a plot of church land.
explanation.definitionFit: Land assigned to a parish clergyman as part of his living came with every benefice.

clue.text: Manifest to all, though above Tommy's head

parts.note: above means over

indicators.note: the head of Tommy's is taken to be its first letter only

explanation.surface: Something plain to everyone except a soldier who cannot grasp it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'above Tommy's head' looks like 'too hard for Tommy' (a Tommy is a British private soldier); read it as OVER placed on top of T.
explanation.definitionFit: Something manifest is open and plain for everyone to see, not hidden.

clue.text: One ascends with flags

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
ascends means rises

explanation.surface: Someone climbing a mountain while carrying flags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flags' looks like banners carried up a hill; it is the gardener's name for the wild yellow iris and its relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Flag is a common name for the iris plant, especially the yellow water iris.

clue.text: Ordered to hold one old horse ? Must be joking !

indicators.note: the word for ordered is made to hold the other pieces inside it

parts.note: bade is the past tense of bid, ordered
one is the Roman numeral I
a nag is an old or worn-out horse

explanation.surface: Someone told to keep hold of an elderly horse and protesting that it must be a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hold' makes the word for ordered contain the numeral and the old horse; 'Must be joking!' is surface exclamation, with only 'joking' defining.
explanation.definitionFit: Badinage is light-hearted teasing banter, a form of joking.

clue.text: Retainer on a country estate

parts.note: a retainer is a servant, and the servant on a country estate who looks after the game birds is the ...

explanation.surface: A loyal servant working on a rural property.
explanation.definitionFit: A servant who guards and tends the game on a country estate is the person in charge of it, the gamekeeper.

clue.text: Press hand-outs ?

parts.note: hand-outs from the press sound like press releases, but the printing press hands out successive printings of a newspaper or book

explanation.surface: Publicity material given to journalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press hand-outs' suggests press releases; read 'press' as the printing press and what it puts out.
explanation.definitionFit: Each issue or printing of a book or newspaper produced by a press is a version that it hands out to readers.
